title: NovaPay v2.0 All-Hands - Feature Flag Strategy
transcript:
[Sarah Chen]: Okay everyone, thanks for joining. Today we're locking in the feature flag strategy for NovaPay v2.0. Priya, can you walk us through the LaunchDarkly setup?

[Priya Nair]: Sure. So we have three flags: MULTI_PROVIDER_ENABLED, BRAINTREE_ACTIVE, and NOVAPAY_V2_CHECKOUT. The idea is we roll out incrementally. First we enable the abstraction layer in production but keep Stripe as the only active provider. Then we flip BRAINTREE_ACTIVE for internal users only. Then gradually roll out to 5%, 25%, 50%, 100% of customers.

[Marcus Rivera]: That rollout plan makes sense for the backend. But Anika, the checkout UI changes are more all-or-nothing, right? We can't show some users the old Stripe flow and others the new generic flow?

[Anika Sharma]: Actually we can, it just needs careful UX. The new checkout component is a drop-in replacement. But yeah, I'd prefer not to have two concurrent checkout UIs in production for more than a week. The edge cases with users mid-checkout during a flag change are gnarly.

[Sarah Chen]: Let's agree that NOVAPAY_V2_CHECKOUT flips for all users at once, on a Tuesday morning when traffic is lowest. Priya, can you coordinate that with the backend rollout timing?

[Priya Nair]: Yes, I'll schedule it. Tuesday 6am IST. I'll send a calendar invite with the rollback plan attached.

[James Okafor]: One thing I want on record: any new payment provider activated via feature flag still has to pass through the GDPR compliance review before the flag goes above 0%. Not after. The feature flag is not a bypass for compliance review.

[Sarah Chen]: Agreed. James, do you want to be a required approver on the LaunchDarkly flag before it can be enabled?

[James Okafor]: Yes please. Add me as an approver for any flag in the 'payments' namespace.

[Marcus Rivera]: Done. I'll update the LaunchDarkly approval workflow today.

[Sarah Chen]: Good. Anything else? ... Okay, let's wrap up. Summary: three-phase rollout, backend first, UI flip all-at-once on Tuesday 6am IST, James is required approver on all payment flags. Priya sends the calendar invite with rollback plan.

title: Data Retention Policy Review - Engineering + Legal
transcript:
[James Okafor]: Thanks for making time. The item on the table is Priya's request to extend retention for ML training data beyond the 90-day limit.

[Priya Nair]: Right. To be clear about what we actually need: our churn prediction model requires at least 6 months of behavioral sequences to be accurate. With 90-day data, the model is guessing on users with long engagement cycles. We're losing ~$200k/year in preventable churn because the model can't see the signal.

[James Okafor]: I hear you on the business cost. My concern is individual-linked data. But I've been thinking about this — if you genuinely anonymize it, it's outside GDPR scope entirely. The question is whether your anonymization is real or nominal.

[Priya Nair]: What would you need to see to be confident it's real anonymization?

[James Okafor]: No user_id, no device fingerprint, no IP. And cohort sizes must be above 100 users so you can't reverse-engineer individuals from small groups. If you replace user_id with a rotating cohort_id that resets monthly, I think that works. But I'd want to see the schema.

[Priya Nair]: That actually gives us what we need. The model works on behavioral patterns, not individual identities. Sarah, does this work from a product perspective?

[Sarah Chen]: Yes, the ML model doesn't need to know WHO churned, just the behavioral patterns. This is fine. James, can you document the exception formally?

[James Okafor]: I'll put it in the GDPR policy Confluence page today and send a summary email to both of you. The exception is specific to the data/ML team and I'll need to review any proposed schema before it's implemented.

title: January Engineering All-Hands
transcript:
[Sarah Chen]: Happy new year everyone. Quick look at Q1 priorities before we get into the weeds. Top three: NovaPay v2.0 launch, the infra migration to ECS Fargate, and getting our GDPR audit-ready for March.

[Priya Nair]: On the ECS Fargate migration — we're moving away from EC2 instances to reduce our ops overhead. All services should be containerized by end of January. Marcus, the payments service is the last one that isn't Dockerized.

[Marcus Rivera]: Yeah, I've been putting it off because of the GDPR-related environment variable handling. Priya, can we talk after this about the secrets management approach for the payments containers? I don't want to bake EU region config into an image.

[Priya Nair]: Yes, we'll use AWS Secrets Manager with the ECS task role. The region config goes in the task definition, not the image. I'll send you the template.

[James Okafor]: The GDPR audit in March will specifically look at our data deletion workflow. Marcus, I'll need a demo of the full deletion flow — request comes in, gets logged, engineering executes the deletion, confirmation sent. Can we schedule a dry run in February?

[Marcus Rivera]: February 20th work for you? I'll have Anika there too for the frontend deletion confirmation email.

[James Okafor]: Works for me. I'll send a calendar invite.

[Anika Sharma]: Quick product thing: I've been getting user feedback that the checkout loading state is confusing — people aren't sure if their payment went through. Can we prioritize a clearer payment status page in Q1?

[Sarah Chen]: Yes, let's add that to NOVA-134. The NovaPay v2.0 frontend work should include this. Anika, file a sub-task under that Jira ticket.
